timeline_observations.statement: Baseline period: checkout request rate ~40 rps and mean request duration ~0.21s while pool utilization under service_version v1 was 0.6-0.7.

Degraded period: from the 10:32 bucket onward, request rate fell to 9 rps, mean request duration rose to ~1.04-1.08s, and pool utilization under service_version v2 was fully occupied at 1.0. Bucket boundaries are not exact onset times.

One synthetic slow-trace discovery result exists at 2026-09-19T10:33:10Z (trace 00000000000000000000000000000001, POST /checkout, 1060.123 ms), consistent with the elevated latency window, but it is a limited match, not a population sample, and no span-level breakdown was retrieved.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Checkout latency rose at ~10:32 coinciding with the appearance of service_version v2, whose connection pool utilization is fully saturated (1.0) versus 0.6-0.7 under v1; a plausible mechanism is that v2 introduced a configuration or behavior change causing connection pool exhaustion and queuing, but the connection-wait mechanism itself was not measured and the role of the concurrent request-rate drop (40 -> 9 rps) is unexplained.
verification_needed: Collect connection_wait_mean_seconds (check-003) to confirm requests actually wait on pool acquisition rather than in query execution or a downstream call.
Retrieve get_trace span breakdowns for slow traces (check-002) to determine where the ~1s is spent; only find_traces discovery data exists.
Obtain pool_limit configuration for v1 and v2 (no configuration evidence was collected) to test whether v2 changed the pool limit.
Explain the simultaneous request-rate drop from 40 to 9 rps: it could be reduced upstream load, throttling, or a consequence of slow responses; current evidence cannot distinguish.
Collection stopped at a controller decision_budget limit, so additional metrics/traces were never gathered; uncertainty remains.

supporting_findings.statement: Mean request duration increased roughly 5x from ~0.21-0.22s (10:30-10:31) to ~1.04-1.08s (10:32-10:34).

Pool utilization for service_version v2 is at the fully-occupied ratio of 1.0 in every degraded-period bucket, while v1 showed 0.6-0.7 in the baseline period; utilization alone does not prove the incident mechanism.
A slow synthetic trace (1060.123 ms) at 10:33:10Z corroborates that individual requests were slow during the degraded window, though it is not a population sample and no spans were retrieved.
Request rate dropped from 40 rps to 9 rps in the same 10:32 bucket where latency and pool saturation changed, coinciding with the label shift from v1 to v2.

contradicting_findings.statement: Saturated pool utilization coincides with a falling request rate (40 -> 9 rps), which is not the classic overload signature of rising load; the rate drop could indicate reduced concurrency or an unobserved bottleneck other than pure load-driven saturation, and it remains unexplained.
